Where We Are in Place and Time · Year 5

Colonial Women

A convict who became one of the richest people in the colony. A woman who met the ships at the wharf and found homes for eleven thousand strangers. A farmer’s daughter who ran a sheep empire while her husband was banished. All three were alive at the same time, in the same small town.

Learning intentionTo use primary and secondary sources to investigate the contributions of significant women in Australia’s past.
Recap, one of three

Eleven ships, eight months

Before we meet the women, a quick reminder of the colony they lived in. The First Fleet left Portsmouth in May 1787 and reached Sydney Cove in January 1788.
780Convicts on board
550Crew, soldiers and their families
Eight months at sea. No engines, no radio, no way of turning back. Over the next eighty years British courts sent more than 160,000 convicts to Australia.
Think
1,330 people arrived. About 1,500 Aboriginal people were counted around the harbour at the time, and historians think that count was far too low. What does that tell you about the size of the colony in its first year?

Talk about it with the person next to you. Nothing to write yet.

Recap, two of three

Why send people here at all?

Britain had a problem at home and thought it had found the answer on the other side of the world. Three reasons, and one very convenient idea.
Sending prisoners overseas was called transportation. It emptied the gaols without building new ones.
A colony far away was somewhere to send people Britain could not feed or employ.
Terra nullius

In 1770 James Cook charted the east coast. He and the botanist Joseph Banks reported that there were few people living along it.

The land was declared terra nullius, Latin for nobody’s land. In British eyes that gave them the legal right to take it.

It was not true. Aboriginal peoples had lived here, cared for the land and belonged to it for tens of thousands of years. Terra nullius was not overturned in Australian law until the Mabo decision in 1992.

Recap, three of three

What happened after they landed

The colony did not stay by the harbour. Within twenty-five years it had pushed over the mountains, and Aboriginal people were being pushed off Country to make room for it.
Relations soured quickly. The colonists and the local peoples shared no language and no customs, and what each expected of the other was impossible to guess. Attacks happened on both sides. But it was disease and the loss of land that harmed Aboriginal communities most heavily.
1813. Blaxland, Wentworth and Lawson found a way through the Blue Mountains. Beyond lay grassland the colony wanted for sheep and cattle.
Look closely
Two large areas of this map are labelled “Countries Unexplored”.
Unexplored by the British. Aboriginal peoples had lived in every part of that blank space for tens of thousands of years, and knew it far better than any mapmaker in London. A map is not a neutral picture. It shows you what the people who drew it knew, wanted, and chose to leave out.

One of three

Mary Reibey

Born Molly Haydock in Lancashire in 1777. Orphaned young. Caught stealing a horse while dressed as a boy. Sent 17,000 kilometres away at fifteen.
I will make my self as happy as I Can In my Pressent and unhappy situation.Mary Reibey to her aunt Penelope Hope, 8 October 1792, the day after she landed. She was fifteen. Her spelling.
What she did. Took over her husband’s ships and stores when he died in 1811 and made the business far bigger. Opened a George Street warehouse in 1812. Traded grain, coal, cedar and wheat. Owned the brig Governor Macquarie. Held about 1,000 acres by 1820.
What it cost. Transported at fifteen with a seven year sentence. Widowed at thirty-four with seven children. She outlived five of them. In 1817 she was convicted of assaulting a man who owed her money, so she was not a saint either.
Read the source
That sentence was written by a fifteen year old the day after she got off a convict ship. What does it tell you about her that a list of her achievements would not?

Talk it through, then write one sentence in your book.

One of three

How Mary Reibey is remembered

She died in 1855 as one of the wealthiest people in the colony. Nearly two centuries later most Australians carry her face in their pocket without knowing whose it is.
Look at the other side. The $20 note also shows an Eora nowie, a bark canoe, with Aboriginal women fishing in the harbour. It was a common sight in Mary Reibey’s lifetime. One small piece of paper holding two stories at once.
What she left. Her face on the $20 note. Reiby Place in Sydney. Figtree House at Hunters Hill, on land she owned, still standing. A governorship of the Sydney Free Grammar School in 1825. And an idea the colony found hard to swallow: that a transported convict girl could end up richer than the people who sentenced her.
Two of three

Caroline Chisholm

She was not sent here and she did not come for land. She came with her soldier husband, saw women sleeping in the streets after months at sea, and decided it was her job to fix it.
I promised to know neither country nor creed, but to try to serve all justly and impartially.Caroline Chisholm, on the Easter Sunday in 1841 when she dedicated herself to the work. Recorded in a memoir published in her lifetime.
64 girls, 14 shillings. She found a group of 64 young women sheltering in the Rocks with fourteen shillings and threepence between all of them.
A home in a barracks. In January 1841 she persuaded Governor Gipps to give her part of the old immigration barracks. It slept up to 96 women and ran the only free job registry in Sydney. It was overrun with rats.
Captain the white horse. Through 1842 she was almost always in the saddle, leading wagon convoys inland and setting up resting stations and job agencies at a dozen country towns.
Her advertising slogan, in her own words: “Comfort for the Poor! Meat Three Times a Day!!” Two exclamation marks. She knew exactly who she was talking to, and what they were hungry for.
Two of three

How Caroline Chisholm is remembered

She helped more than eleven thousand people, then died poor in London lodgings in 1877, largely forgotten. It took Australia about sixty years to build her a proper memorial.
Named after her: a federal electorate, a Canberra suburb, a TAFE, a university college and several schools in both Australia and England. She also came to believe that everyone should be allowed to vote, that votes should be secret, and that members of parliament should be paid so ordinary people could stand. All three are now Australian law.
Think about it
She was famous in the 1840s, forgotten by the 1860s, and famous again a century later. Why can a person be forgotten and then remembered?

Who decides which names go on money, streets and schools?

Three of three

Elizabeth Macarthur

A Devon farmer’s daughter who arrived free, not in chains, and then ran a sheep empire for eight and a half years while her husband was banished to the other side of the world.
having no female friend to unbend my mind to, nor a single woman with whom I could converse.Elizabeth Macarthur to her friend Bridget Kingdon, 7 March 1791, on her first months in the colony.
What she did. Ran the family’s farms from 1809 to 1817 while John was banished. Chose which rams to breed from, supervised shearing and baling, kept the accounts, directed convict workers, and sent inspection reports to England.
What she learned. A ship’s surgeon left her his piano and taught her to play; the first tune she managed was “God Save the King”. An officer who studied the stars taught her to classify plants. In 1795 she wrote home that they had fifty cattle, a dozen horses and about a thousand sheep.
Say it accurately. She did not do it alone. Her husband’s nephew Hannibal helped, and later her sons. John sent letters of advice from England, which she often ignored, because she was the one who could actually see the sheep.
Three of three

How Elizabeth Macarthur is remembered

Her house is still standing and you can walk through it. Her husband went on the $2 note. She has never appeared on Australian money.
Named after her: Elizabeth Farm itself, the Elizabeth Macarthur Agricultural Institute at Menangle, and Elizabeth Macarthur High School. Her letters survive at the State Library of New South Wales, and volunteers are still transcribing them, so the record of her life is not finished yet.
The hard question
For over a century John Macarthur was called the father of the Australian wool industry and Elizabeth was barely mentioned. Historians now say that is wrong, and that neither of them started it. Why was the story told that way for so long?

Write your answer in your book. There is more than one good reason.

Station 05

Careful, historians

Every one of these gets said about these three women. Some are true and some are not. Tap each card to turn it over, then be careful not to put the wrong ones in your book.
A good historian is not the one who knows the most facts. It is the one who checks where a fact came from before repeating it.
Station 06

Whose Country was this?

All three of these women built their lives on land that already belonged to somebody. An honest investigation holds both things at once: what she achieved, and what it cost the people who were already here.

Mary Reibey

Dyarubbin, the Hawkesbury River. Darug and Darkinjung Country. The Reibeys farmed there and ran grain boats up and down the river from the mid 1790s.

Between 1794 and 1816 that river was the site of one of the longest and most brutal frontier wars in Australian history. The money that started her fortune came out of those riverlands.

And: Darug and Darkinjung people never disappeared from Dyarubbin. They are still there today, and in recent years Darug knowledge holders have been recovering and telling the river’s own names and stories.

Caroline Chisholm

Shellharbour is Dharawal Country. The Wodi Wodi people, part of the Dharawal nation, have lived there for thousands of years. Bass Point, just south of the harbour, is one of the two most important archaeological sites on the New South Wales coast.

In December 1843 Chisholm brought 23 families there by steamer to start farms.

Both are true. She was helping poor families who had nothing. The land she helped them onto was taken from families who were already there.

Elizabeth Macarthur

Elizabeth Farm stands on Dharug Country. Camden Park sits where Dharawal, Gundungurra and Dharug Country meet. The district’s own name was Benkennie, meaning dry land.

Sheep need grassland. The Macarthur grants ran to tens of thousands of acres of it.

The museum says so itself. Museums of History NSW acknowledges Parramatta’s part in the control of Aboriginal people, and names Hannibal Macarthur, who helped Elizabeth run the farms, as a member of the committee that governed the Native Institution.

Hold two ideas at once
Choose one of the three women. In your book, write two sentences: one about something she achieved that you admire, and one about the cost of it to Aboriginal people. Then write a third sentence answering this: does the second sentence cancel out the first?

There is no correct answer. There is a well-argued one and a lazy one.

Something to look at In the garden at Elizabeth Farm today there is an artwork by Tony Albert, a Kuku Yalanji artist. It is a wooden nursery four metres high and eight metres across, filled with woven baskets made by artists from four Aboriginal art centres, and planted with native plants. It stands on the Macarthurs’ own ground. Albert called it a work “full of love and reflection”.

Before you finish

Check your book has all of this in it:

One last thought Three women, born within forty-two years of each other, living in the same small colony. One arrived in chains, one arrived free and rich, one arrived by choice to help other people. All three ended up changing the place. What does that tell you about who gets to matter in history, and who decides?
